sections.brief: Open the volume's diplomacy where Volume II's Truman section stops ([scene:tr_s02|Truman after the money]): Israel's doctrine of non-identification from Ben-Gurion's 27 September 1948 statement and the 9 March 1949 Basic Principles ('in particular with the United States and the Soviet Union'), Comay's summary and Sharett's 'knocking on every door', ending with the recognition of the People's Republic of China on 9 January 1950 and Shichor's account of why no relations followed (Zhou's July 1951 refusal; US pressure 'even using threats'; ties only in 1992). Explain the term as policy, not ideology, with Shlaim's reading labelled as interpretation, and keep the Korean decision for cw1_korea. Figure: timeline September 1948–January 1950.

The founding of Israel's intelligence community, June 1948–1952, in order: the dissolution of the Haganah Intelligence Service on 30 June 1948 and the three successors (Aman, the Foreign Ministry's Political Division, the internal service under Harel that became the Shin Bet); the legal anchoring of 18 February 1949 and the secrecy until 1957 (single source, attribute it); Ben-Gurion's secret directive of 13 December 1949 creating the coordinating institute under Shiloah, reporting to the prime minister, with its IL20,000 budget and IL5,000 for special operations needing his prior approval; Shiloah's 2 March 1951 'Directorate' order, the 1 April 1951 reorganization, the 1951 Baghdad exposure, and Harel's succession in 1952 as the 'Memuneh' over both services. From s19h tell only the structural point that the Mossad answers to the prime minister alone (its founding directive shows this from the start) and link forward for its later operations and the 2025 findings; do not retell the 2024–26 material. Figure: power structure of the intelligence community as created 1948–1952 (Prime Minister, Defence/IDF, Foreign Ministry), from the cited entries.

The Tripartite Declaration of 25 May 1950 read from the text, paragraph by paragraph (arms for internal security and self-defence; assurances of non-aggression; 'unalterable opposition to the use of force' and action within and outside the UN against violation of frontiers or armistice lines), then the policy behind it: NSC 65/3 (19 May 1950) and the 7 August 1950 progress report's arms rule. Present the reception from both sides and the dispute: the US report that Israel was 'pleased' and saw itself recognized as 'a permanent element in the Near East', against Ben-Gurion's diary of 30 May 1950 (via Shlaim) accusing it of arming the Arab states; the Arab press complaint that it 'froze' the status quo and the Arab League's 12 June commentary; Malik's questions and Hare's 'no intent to recognize spheres of influence'. Link back to [scene:tr_s02|Truman's 1948–50 decisions] in one sentence. Figure: comparison of the three paragraphs (what each committed, to whom, with what enforcement).

The decisive break, June 1950–May 1951: the cabinet discussion of 2 July 1950 at Weizmann's home, the 7 July statement, Ben-Gurion's 4 July Knesset defence of the vote ('a vote for the United Nations'), no troops but $100,000 in food and medicine, the Peace Observation Commission and the seven-point plan, Maki's dissent; then Ben-Gurion's late-July offer to the US ambassador of a 250,000-man army 'capable and anxious' to aid the West, and his May 1951 US visit (note the 3–8 May vs 31 May discrepancy in the State Department listing). Present the dispute over why Israel tilted (Brecher's arms-and-aid reading and Shlaim's three reasons against the establishment view that Moscow pushed Israel away), each labelled as interpretation. Close by pointing to cw1_soviet_break for the rupture. Figure: timeline June 1950–May 1951.

Iran's oil nationalization and the Anglo-Iranian crisis, told from 1941 (briefly, from me_s06) and in full for 1949–July 1952: the First Development Plan and the 1949 elections, the November 1950 committee vote under Mossadeq, Razmara's assassination, the 15 March 1951 nationalization vote and Mossadeq's appointment, Britain's ICJ case (26 May 1951; provisional measures 5 July 1951; no jurisdiction 22 July 1952, with the dissenters), the Harriman and Stokes missions, the September 1951 sterling freeze and embargo, the collapse of production from 242 million barrels (1950) to 10.6 million (1952) from me_s06, the July 1952 resignation and reinstatement, full powers, the Truman–Churchill message, Byroade's September 1952 judgment, and the October 1952 break with Britain. Present the ICJ dispute (Library of Congress 'in Iran's favour' vs the Court's own no-jurisdiction ruling) and correct the common Time 'Man of the Year' framing with Time's own words. Stop before the August 1953 plebiscite and coup (told in s11). Map: me_layers; figure: timeline 1949–October 1952.

The first Security Council crisis on the Syrian front, March–September 1951, picking up from Volume II's Syria section ([scene:rd6_syria_1949|Syria in 1949]): Syria's complaints and reasons, Israel's case (drainage since October 1950, El Hamma on 4 April with seven policemen killed, the 5 April air action, the claim of sovereignty), Resolution 93 of 18 May 1951 (10–0–1, the USSR abstaining), the Chief of Staff's finding that neither party held sovereignty, the 785 civilians evacuated and about 260 who chose to return (Palestinian citizens of the zone, named as such), Tel el Mutilla and the UN's later finding of Syrian army participation. Present Eban's strongest case and Syria's on equal terms, and the sovereignty dispute. Link forward to [scene:sy_s02|the demilitarized zones and the water war] for 1953–67. Figure: timeline 29 March–23 September 1951; key figures (7 policemen; 785 evacuated; 632 interviewed; about 260 returned; 10–0–1).

How the first US grant aid was won, March 1951–June 1952, picking up from [scene:rd6_financing|how the new state was paid for] and not retelling the CRS table: the March 1951 Eban–Horowitz note for $150 million (with its 510,000 and 600,000 figures and the parallel $1.5 billion reparations request), the Douglas–Taft and McCormack bills and their Cold War language ('a bulwark' against Communist threats 'particularly in Iran'), the Administration's $23.5 million and the State Department's resistance (McGhee's memo, the Feinberg and Blaustein approaches), the Senate's Douglas amendment, and the outcome; then the fiscal 1953 round ($76 million asked, $70,228,000 plus $2,772,000 agreed; the 20% vs under-8% cuts). Set the parallel Arab-refugee money beside it ($25,450,000 in FY1951, $50 million in FY1952, $65 million asked for FY1953). Present the FY1952 figure dispute ($65 million vs about $68.8 million authorized) and, from iaa_s01, only its point that aid stayed economic, not military, until the 1960s, linking forward. Embed aid_arms:Overview:2 and discuss its first step (economic aid and loans only, 1948–1961); figure: money chain (Congress → Mutual Security appropriation → Israeli immigrant absorption → who gained → the cost and the State Department's objection), sourced only to the cited entries.

The lobby in its Cold War frame, 1950–1954, without retelling Volume II's organizational history ([scene:s07g|From AZEC to AIPAC], one linking sentence): Kenen's path (AECZA 1943, Jewish Agency at the UN 1947–48, Israel's first UN delegation 1949), Eban's suggestion that he go to Washington, his refugee-framework argument, his 1951 letter to Silver on the Senate amendment (Douglas, Taft, Brewster, Julius Klein), and the founding dates as each source gives them. Present the founding-date dispute (1951 committee / 1954 AIPAC per JTA vs 1954 AZCPA / 1959 AIPAC per JVL; rd6 gives 1953–54) and say what each refers to. Give American Jewish positions fairly: the Ben-Gurion–Blaustein exchange of 23 August 1950 on allegiance, and the American Council for Judaism's opposition. State plainly that the 1953 founding and the Iran coup share a year and nothing documented connects them (s11's own discipline). Figure: timeline 1943–1959 of Kenen and the committee's names, marking where sources differ.

How intelligence ties with Washington began, 1951 onward, told only to its start: the CIA's initial view of Israel as within the Soviet sphere, Ben-Gurion's 1951 meeting with Bedell Smith, Angleton put in charge of the US side with Manor and Kollek as counterparts, and Shiloah's undated Western contacts. From df_s04 tell only its 1951 origin claim and its discipline that a shared hub is not a pipeline; correct its dating with the dispute: df_s04's 'formal liaison in 1951 under counterintelligence chief Angleton' against Robarge (CIA historian: Angleton headed the Counterintelligence Staff only from 1954; his control of the Israel account 'an administrative anomaly') and McConnell ('how early is a matter of dispute'; the no-covert-operations understanding a mid-1950s effort). From nsa_s01 take only the 1952 founding of Unit 8200 under Aman (attribute; flagged unverified) and link forward for 2006. Mention the 1956 Khrushchev speech in one forward sentence linking [scene:cia_s02|the CIA in 1948] and Stage Two. Figure: comparison of the three accounts of the liaison's start.

Egypt's restrictions on Israel-bound shipping and Resolution 95 of 1 September 1951: the resolution's findings ('of a permanent character'; 'an abuse of the exercise of the right of visit, search and seizure'; no party 'actively a belligerent') and demand, the 8–0–3 vote (China, India and the USSR abstaining). Give Egypt's legal case at full strength from Gross (continuing belligerency, the 1950 regulations, the Constantinople Convention not binding toward a non-signatory, the Council's competence, sabotage) and Fawzi's words, against Eban's and Ecuador's arguments, and present the dispute without resolving it beyond what the resolution itself decided. Link forward to Stage Three for 1956. Figure: comparison of the Egyptian and Council positions on four questions (state of war, visit and search, the Convention, the Council's authority).

Western regional defence and Israel's place outside it, February 1951–1953: Robertson's visit (19 February 1951) and Ben-Gurion's 'insulting proposal' and 'as if they were Australia or New Zealand', Morrison's reply of 23 April 1951, the Middle East Command invitation to Egypt (13 October 1951), Egypt's abrogation of the 1936 treaty and rejection (15 October), Acheson's 'without validity', the separate approach to Israel ('give most serious consideration'), and the idea's fading by 1953. Keep the 1952 Egyptian revolution to one forward sentence (Stage Two). Show the mechanism: who was invited, who was informed, and why (convergence, not conspiracy: British base interests, Egyptian sovereignty, Israel's wish for full membership). Figure: power structure of the proposed Middle East Command (sponsors, invited founding member, states merely informed).

The refugee question after Lausanne ([scene:lau_s01|Lausanne, 1949], one linking sentence), 1950–1953: UNRWA's first year (Beirut headquarters, five districts including Israel, staff numbers, Blandford's arrival 4 July 1951, the contributions table with the US $27,450,000 and Israel $50,000), Truman's 27 July 1951 letter, the Paris conference of 13 September–19 November 1951 with all five proposals, the Refugee Office valuation (£P100 million, about $280 million; 16,324 sq km, 4,574 cultivable), each side's answers in its own words, and the Commission's verdict that neither would 'recede'; Resolution 513's $50 million relief and $200 million reintegration 'without prejudice' to paragraph 11; the Sinai siphon scheme of June 1953 (60,000 refugees, $30 million) and refugee opposition, linking forward to Gaza in 1955. Give Palestinian political agency its place: Arafat's Students League (1951; president from 1952) and Habash's path from Lydda to the Amman clinic (1952), with the dispute over when the Arab Nationalist Movement was founded. Present the Paris dispute from both sides with equal care and name Israel's Iraqi blocked-accounts condition (link [scene:rd6_exodus|the Jews of the Arab world]).

The American home front of the alignment, told to 1953 with one forward paragraph: the Knights of Columbus resolution of 22 April 1951, the 1952 state councils and the Supreme Council's 21 August 1952 call, the 20 August 1953 repetition to every member of Congress and the seventeen House resolutions; then, briefly and as a forward link to Stage Two, Rabaut's resolution, the 14 June 1954 signing and the House and Senate reports' anti-communist language. Present the motive dispute (Cold War contrast in the committee reports vs Kruse's reading of a business-funded campaign against the New Deal, with Spiritual Mobilization's 17,000 ministers and the 1951 DeMille ceremony), each labelled. State plainly that no documented link to Israel or to Zionist organizations appears in these sources; any such reading would be interpretation and is not made here. Note the 1952 vs 1953 date conflict for the National Fraternal Congress. Figure: timeline April 1951–June 1954.

From patron to rupture, 1947–July 1953: the partition vote and the Czech arms (Bialer via Shlaim), the 9 December 1949 Jerusalem vote, then the Slánský trial (arrest November 1951; 14 tried, 11 sentenced to death, executed 3 December 1952; 12 of 14 Jewish per JTA; Avriel, Ben-Gurion and Sharett named; Mordecai Oren's confession used), the Doctors' Plot (13 January 1953; nine doctors, at least six Jewish; the CIA's July 1953 analysis and New Times' 'spy ring' charge), Sharett's 19 January speech, the 9 February legation bombing and the Tzrifin Underground, the break of 11 February (Vyshinsky's 1 a.m. note), Stalin's death, the April exoneration, and restoration on 21 July 1953 after Israel's no-alliance pledge. Name the antisemitism of the trial and the plot plainly, as the sources do, and keep it tied to named states and officials. Present the dispute over who drove the rupture (Sharett's 'developmental logic' vs Bialer). Figure: timeline November 1951–July 1953.

The new administration's line, May–July 1953: Dulles's Near East trip and his 1 June 1953 report (DSB 15 June, pp. 831–835) as reported at the time ('allay the deep resentment', Arab fear of Israeli 'aggressive expansion', Israel to become 'a part of the Near East community', the Tripartite Declaration upheld, 'impartial' policy, Jerusalem's religious claims, refugees mostly to be integrated in Arab countries), then the 28 July 1953 US statement regretting the Foreign Ministry's move to Jerusalem (after objections in July 1952 and March 1953). Present how each side read 'impartiality' only as far as the sources go, and say the reported quotations come from a contemporary newspaper account of the address, not the Bulletin text. Link forward to Stage Two for the September 1953 aid suspension and Qibya, and back to [scene:rd6_un_admission|Jerusalem in 1949–50]. Figure: comparison of the Truman-era and Dulles-era statements on Israel and the Arab states, from the cited entries only.

The coup of August 1953 in full, from s11 and ira_s00 and the primary record: inception in mid-May, Churchill's approval on 1 July, the approval dispute (June 25 per Roosevelt's memoir and the Library of Congress vs 11 July per the CIA memorandum; 'No written authorization from the President has been found'), the conditions Eisenhower and Dulles set, the money ($1,000,000 budget of 4 April 1953; $5,330,000 grand total across three phases; Risen's $5 million to Zahedi; at least $50,000 beforehand), the plebiscite of 3 August, Zahedi's appointment, the failed 14–15 August attempt, the evacuation advice Roosevelt ignored, 19 August, some 300 dead, Mossadeq's trial and house arrest, Fatemi's execution, and the record's long concealment (the 1989 FRUS volume, the 2013 release, the 2017 volume, the destroyed cables). Correct s11's '~$5M cost' with the documented budget figures, and present both disputes (approval date; Anglo-American vs Iranian agency and oil vs Soviet fear) from both sides. From ira_src_s19 give the two historians' positions on the counterfactual, clearly labelled as interpretation. Tell s11's AZCPA half in one sentence linking [scene:cw1_lobby|the lobby's founding] and [scene:s07g|From AZEC to AIPAC], keep its 2024–26 Congress material out except as a forward link, and link forward to [scene:ira_s00b|the 1954 consortium and SAVAK] for SAVAK (whose Mossad role is not established for 1957 by these sources). Figures: process flow of the operation (approval → funding → plebiscite → Zahedi named → failed attempt → 19 August → new government); key figures ($1,000,000; $5,330,000; some 300 dead; 60 years to acknowledgement).

Israel and the coup: participant or beneficiary, 1947–1953, as the chapter's Iranian closing section. Tell Iran's record toward Israel in order (UNSCOP and the 29 November 1947 vote, the 11 May 1949 vote, Sayqal in March 1949, de facto recognition on 6 March 1950 without announcement, Safinia's credentials, the 7 July 1951 consulate closure under Mossadeq citing 'financial difficulties'), then the first economic ties of 1953 (the 11 June bank credit line before the coup; IRIS), and state sq_s01's finding plainly: no documented Israeli role in the coup. Carry the beneficiary claims forward only as far as the sources date them (oil purchases from 1957; Bakhtiar's offer to Zur in September 1957; the periphery concept in the late 1950s) and flag that s11's 'Mossad-trained SAVAK from 1957' is not established by these sources, linking Stage Four. Link [scene:ira_src_s16|Iran's Jewish community] in one sentence. Figure: timeline 1947–1953 of Iran's steps toward and away from Israel.
